title: Bond, tax and spending measures: who paid for the campaign and who was paid from the fund
question: For each local bond or dedicated-fund measure since 2014 that can be followed into the payment file, who funded the campaign for it, how much of the fund's spending can be seen by payee, and how many campaign donors were later paid from it?
finding: 16 measures could be followed: 11 bonds and 5 dedicated funds. Their campaigns raised $27.4 million; the payment file shows $5.33 billion paid from funds named for them, $16.9 million of it before July 2018 and the rest since. 35 organizations and firms gave $1.0 million to those campaigns and were later paid $383.0 million from the same measures' funds; the measure with most such money is the Dignity Fund for seniors and adults with disabilities (15 donors, paid $175.5 million, 34.5% of what the file shows paid from the fund).
how: A measure is included when the City's payment file has a fund named for it: bond funds carry the bond's year and an abbreviation of its title, and three special funds carry the proposition in their name; two renewed funds are matched through the committee's name. Bond names, vote dates, authorized and spent amounts come from the Controller's bond table. Supporting committees were picked by reading committee names (the letter and the subject) and are kept only if the name carries the measure and, for bonds, most of the money arrived in the 400 days before the vote. Campaign money is every contribution on the committees' Schedule A and C. Where a committee's name gives only a letter, the measure's title is confirmed from titles other committees typed on their own filings, or from the name the committee was given on Form 114.5. Payees are everyone the payment file shows paid from the fund; the file holds the lines filed under fiscal 2019 to 2027 to date, and the fiscal years shown are the years the payments were issued, read from their voucher numbers. 'Share visible' is the fund dollars seen in the payment file against the bond money the Controller reports spent; the bond table runs to fiscal 2024-25 and the payments to November 2026, so a recent bond can show more than 100% and the share is left blank where the payments are more than half as large again as the table's figure.
limits: For most of these, funding a measure and then being paid from it is unsurprising: the firms that build fire stations support earthquake bonds and the charities that serve seniors campaigned for the seniors' fund. Bond contracts are bid, and grants from the funds are awarded by departments, not by the campaign. The payment file begins in July 2018, so earlier spending from the 2014 to 2016 bonds is missing apart from $16.9 million that was issued earlier and filed under a later year, and transport and seawall bond money is spent through the transit and port funds, where it cannot be told from other money (their 'share visible' is close to nothing). Housing bond money is paid to a separate partnership for each building, so a developer that gave under its own name will usually not match the payee. Measures whose money goes into the general fund (most taxes) cannot be followed at all. Opposing committees and independent spending are not included. The payment file labels each line with a fiscal year that is not always the year the payment was issued: some earlier payments, mostly on purchase orders in multi-year capital funds, are filed under a later year, and the Controller's own published figures follow that label. Payments are dated here by voucher number, a single running sequence, which moves $5.52 billion of $119.3 billion (4.6%) to an earlier year than its label; $1.08 billion of that belongs to fiscal 2018 or earlier, before the file starts. Near the turn of a year the number dates a payment to within a few days.
